**Answer: No.**

A poset can have antichains of arbitrarily large finite size yet contain no infinite antichain. Here is a counterexample.

**Construction.** Let
$$P = \{(n,k) : n \in \mathbb{N}^+,\; 1 \le k \le n\},$$
with the partial order
$$(n,k) \le (m,\ell) \iff n \le m \text{ and } k \le \ell.$$

This is reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive, so $(P,\le)$ is a poset.

**Arbitrarily large finite antichains.** For each $t \ge 1$, consider
$$A_t = \{(t+i-1,\; t-i+1) : 1 \le i \le t\} = \{(t,t),\, (t+1,t-1),\, \ldots,\, (2t-1,1)\}.$$
Each element $(t+i-1,\, t-i+1)$ satisfies $1 \le t-i+1 \le t+i-1$, so $A_t \subseteq P$.

Take two distinct elements $(n,k),(m,\ell) \in A_t$ with $n < m$ (so the first coordinates are strictly increasing while the second coordinates are strictly decreasing). Then $k > \ell$, which means $(n,k) \not\le (m,\ell)$ (since $k \not\le \ell$), and $(m,\ell) \not\le (n,k)$ (since $m \not\le n$). Hence no two elements of $A_t$ are comparable, so $A_t$ is an antichain of size $t$. Since $t$ is arbitrary, $P$ has antichains of arbitrarily large size.

**No infinite antichain.** Suppose for contradiction that $B \subseteq P$ is an infinite antichain. Since each "level" $\{(n,k):1\le k\le n\}$ is totally ordered (hence contains at most one element of any antichain), $B$ must contain elements with infinitely many distinct first coordinates. List them as $(n_1,k_1),(n_2,k_2),\ldots$ with $n_1 < n_2 < n_3 < \cdots$ (choosing a strictly increasing subsequence of first coordinates, which exists since they are infinitely many distinct positive integers).

For $i < j$ we have $n_i < n_j$. Since $B$ is an antichain, $(n_i,k_i) \not\le (n_j,k_j)$, which (given $n_i \le n_j$) forces $k_i \not\le k_j$, i.e., $k_i > k_j$. Thus
$$k_1 > k_2 > k_3 > \cdots \ge 1,$$
a strictly decreasing infinite sequence of positive integers — impossible. Contradiction.

Therefore $P$ has no infinite antichain, even though it has antichains of every finite size.

### PROOF COMPLETE
